items.prompt: How does a bat find flying insects in complete darkness?

options.label: It relies on unusually sharp night vision
options.feedback: Many bats that hunt this way have quite weak eyesight; darkness would defeat vision alone regardless of how sharp it was.

options.label: It reads the echoes of its own high-pitched calls
options.feedback: By timing and comparing the echoes that bounce back off nearby objects, a bat builds a detailed picture of everything around it, including a moving insect, without needing any light at all.

options.label: It follows scent trails left by insects
options.feedback: Insects in open flight leave little trail to follow, and a bat's hunting calls would be pointless if scent alone were doing the work.

options.label: It senses the warmth given off by the insect's body
options.feedback: An insect's body gives off far too little heat to detect at any distance; that sense belongs to a different kind of hunter entirely.

items.ok_line: A picture of the world built entirely from returning sound.
items.ko_line: Think about what the bat is sending out, not what it might be able to see or smell.
items.exp_title: Seeing with sound instead of light
items.exp_text: A hunting bat sends out a stream of very high-pitched calls, far above what a human ear can register, and listens for the faint echoes that bounce back off everything nearby. The time each echo takes to return reveals how far away an object is, and small differences between the echoes reaching each ear reveal its direction, so the bat builds a detailed, constantly updated picture of its surroundings from sound alone. As it closes in on a moving insect, it speeds up its calls to refine that picture right up to the final instant of the catch.

items.prompt: How can a shark find a fish hiding completely buried under the sand?

options.label: It smells the fish through the sand
options.feedback: Scent spreads too slowly and unevenly through packed sand to pinpoint an exact hiding spot the way a shark manages to.

options.label: It hears the fish's heartbeat
options.feedback: A heartbeat produces no sound that travels through sand and water in a way any ear could pick up.

options.label: It feels vibrations through its skin alone
options.feedback: Vibration sensing works well in open water over some distance, but a motionless fish buried in sand produces almost no vibration to detect.

options.label: It detects the faint electrical field the fish's muscles give off
options.feedback: Special jelly-filled pores on the shark's snout sense the tiny electrical signals every living muscle produces, revealing the fish's location even with no other clue showing.

items.ok_line: Every twitch of muscle gives off a signal the shark can pick up.
items.ko_line: Think about what a living body gives off even while it lies perfectly still.
items.exp_text: Every time a muscle in an animal's body contracts, including the small movements of breathing or a beating heart, it produces a faint electrical signal. A shark's snout is covered in tiny pores, each connected to a jelly-filled canal, that are sensitive enough to detect signals of that size from very close range. That sense lets a shark zero in on a fish hidden under sand or mud with no smell, sound, or sight of it reaching the shark at all.

items.prompt: How does a pit viper strike accurately at warm-blooded prey on a pitch-black night?

options.label: Heat-sensing pits on its face detect body warmth
options.feedback: A pair of small pits between the eyes and nostrils are lined with membrane so sensitive to heat that they build a rough picture of a nearby warm body, day or night alike.

options.label: It tastes the air for warm scent particles
options.feedback: The snake's tongue does sample chemical particles in the air, but that sense works alongside the pits and is separate from detecting heat itself.

options.label: Its eyes see unusually well in darkness
options.feedback: Even snakes with weak eyesight can strike accurately in total darkness using their pits, showing that sight is not what is doing the work here.

options.label: It listens for the prey's breathing
options.feedback: Snakes have no external ears and are not especially sensitive to airborne sound of that kind; this ability works even for prey that makes no sound.

items.ok_line: A picture built from warmth reaching a sensitive pit, not from light.
items.ko_line: Look at the small pit between the eye and nostril, and think about what it might sense.
items.exp_title: A picture built from warmth, not light
items.exp_text: Between each eye and nostril, a pit viper has a small pit lined with a membrane packed full of heat-sensitive nerve endings. Warmth radiating off a nearby animal's body strikes that membrane and is translated into signals the brain can combine with what the eyes see, or use entirely on its own in full darkness. That heat-built picture is precise enough to guide the strike to the right spot even when there is no light to see by at all.

items.prompt: What lets a dog follow a scent trail that is completely invisible to a person?

options.label: A dog's nose is simply larger than a person's
options.feedback: Size alone is not the reason; the difference lies in the structures packed inside the nose, not how big it looks from outside.

options.label: Dogs can see faint traces left in the air
options.feedback: A scent trail is chemical, not visual; nothing about it could be picked out by eyesight, however good.

options.label: A much larger area inside the nose is lined with scent receptors
options.feedback: Tightly folded tissue packs a vastly greater surface of scent-detecting cells into a dog's nose than fits into a person's, letting it register chemical traces far too faint for us to notice at all.

options.label: Dogs remember smells better, not detect them better
options.feedback: Memory plays a part after a scent is noticed, but a dog can also detect a trail a person's nose could never register in the first place, no matter how well that person remembered smells.

items.ok_line: Not a bigger nose so much as a nose folded to pack in far more receptors.
items.ko_line: Think about what is folded up inside the nose, not its outward size.
items.exp_title: A nose built for chemical detail
items.exp_text: Inside a dog's nose, the tissue that detects scent is folded and creased so tightly that it packs a very large surface area of scent receptors into a small space, far more than fits inside a human nose of similar size. Air pulled in during a sniff is also drawn across this surface in a separate path from ordinary breathing, so the receptors get a concentrated sample rather than a diluted one. That combination lets a dog register chemical traces at concentrations a person's nose simply has no way to notice.

items.prompt: How does an owl pinpoint the exact location of a mouse rustling under snow, in total darkness?

options.label: It relies on extremely sharp eyesight
options.feedback: The prey here is hidden from sight entirely, under snow or cover, so vision cannot be what locates it.

options.label: Its ears are positioned unevenly on its head
options.feedback: Because one ear opening sits slightly higher than the other, a sound reaches them at a tiny difference in time and loudness, and the brain uses that difference to calculate the sound's exact direction.

options.label: It sniffs out the mouse's scent through snow
options.feedback: Owls have a comparatively poor sense of smell, and this kind of precise strike works even when there is no scent trail to follow at all.

options.label: It feels vibrations in the snow through its feet
options.feedback: The strike is aimed before the owl ever lands, from well above the snow, ruling out anything felt underfoot.

items.ok_line: Lopsided ears turn a tiny timing gap into an exact direction.
items.ko_line: The prey cannot be seen or smelled here; think about what the ears alone might manage.
items.exp_text: In many owls, the two ear openings sit at slightly different heights and angles on the skull, one a little higher and angled differently than the other. A sound from below reaches the lower ear a fraction sooner and slightly louder than it reaches the higher one, and the brain compares those tiny differences to work out the sound's direction with real precision. Facial feathers arranged in a shallow dish also help funnel sound toward the ears, sharpening that picture enough to guide a silent dive straight onto prey it cannot see.

items.prompt: How can a male moth find a single female from a great distance away in the dark?

options.label: He follows a sound only moths can hear
options.feedback: This kind of long-distance search relies on a chemical signal drifting on the air, not on any sound the female produces.

options.label: He can see her wing pattern from far off
options.feedback: At the distances involved, a moth's eyes could not resolve any pattern at all; something else has to be doing the finding.

options.label: He waits for her to fly to him instead
options.feedback: In this pairing it is typically the male that travels toward the female's signal, following it upwind rather than staying put.

options.label: Feathery antennae detect her scent in tiny traces
options.feedback: His antennae are covered in receptors tuned to one particular scent, sensitive enough to catch a handful of scent molecules drifting on the wind and follow that faint trail back to its source.

items.ok_line: A scent thinned almost to nothing, and antennae built to catch it anyway.
items.ko_line: Think about what drifts on the wind long after the source has moved on.
items.exp_title: Following a scent thinned almost to nothing
items.exp_text: A female moth releases a chemical signal into the air that spreads and thins with distance until only the faintest trace remains far downwind. A male's antennae are broad and feathery, covered with a dense array of receptors built to respond to that one particular scent and almost nothing else, which lets them register even a trace of scent molecules reaching him on the breeze. Turning to fly upwind whenever the scent strengthens and adjusting course whenever it fades, he narrows in on her location step by step.

items.prompt: How does a fish sense a predator approaching from behind without seeing or hearing it?

options.label: A line of sensors along its body detects water movement
options.feedback: A row of tiny receptors running down each side of the body picks up subtle changes in water pressure and flow caused by anything moving nearby, from any direction.

options.label: It relies entirely on eyesight
options.feedback: This sense works even directly behind the fish, outside its field of view, and even in murky water where sight would fail.

options.label: It tastes chemicals released by the predator
options.feedback: A chemical taste trail would take real time to build up and spread; this sense responds to something happening almost instantly.

options.label: It feels the vibration through the bones in its skull alone
options.feedback: The sensing structure runs the length of the body, not just through the skull, which is why a fish can detect movement anywhere nearby, not only close to its head.

items.ok_line: A whole side of the body wired to feel the water itself moving.
items.ko_line: Think about a sense that runs the length of the fish's body, not just its head.
items.exp_text: Running along each side of a fish's body is a line of small canals, just under the skin, packed with sensory cells that respond to the slightest shift in surrounding water. Any moving object nearby, whether a predator closing in or another fish swimming past, disturbs the water in a pattern this line can pick up, even from directions the fish cannot see. That shared sense is also what lets a large school turn together almost as one body, each fish reading the water disturbed by its neighbours rather than watching them directly.

items.prompt: How does a star-nosed mole identify food in complete darkness faster than most animals could even see it?

options.label: It relies on an exceptional sense of smell
options.feedback: Its nose is built for touch rather than scent, and this animal's most striking ability comes from feeling rather than smelling its surroundings.

options.label: It uses echolocation like a bat
options.feedback: This mole makes no such calls; the picture it builds of its surroundings comes from touch, not from sound bouncing back.

options.label: Fleshy tentacles around its nose feel everything nearby
options.feedback: A ring of small, mobile, touch-sensitive tentacles surrounds each nostril and brushes rapidly over the ground ahead, and each one reports back with enough detail that the mole can tell food from dirt almost the instant it makes contact.

options.label: It has unusually sharp eyesight suited to darkness
options.feedback: Living underground, this mole has very poor eyesight and depends on an entirely different sense to find its way and its food.

items.ok_line: A ring of tentacles doing the work eyes would do in the light.
items.ko_line: Look at what surrounds this mole's nostrils, rather than at the nose itself.
items.exp_title: A nose that reads the ground by touch
items.exp_text: A star-nosed mole's nose ends in a ring of small, fleshy tentacles, each one packed with touch-sensitive nerve endings and constantly twitching over the surface just ahead as the mole moves. Because so much nerve tissue is devoted to processing signals from these tentacles, the brain can identify what each one has brushed against almost as soon as contact is made, well before a slower sense could finish checking the same ground. Working almost entirely underground and often underwater, in complete darkness, this touch-built picture stands in for the eyes the mole barely needs at all.

items.prompt: How does a bee find the exact centre of a flower so quickly among a mass of petals?

options.label: It follows a trail of scent straight to the nectar
options.feedback: Scent does help draw a bee toward a flower generally, but finding the precise centre relies on something the bee can see rather than smell.

options.label: It sees ultraviolet patterns invisible to us
options.feedback: Many flowers carry markings that only show up in ultraviolet light, forming a bold path that points straight toward the nectar, and a bee's eyes can see that path plainly even though ours cannot.

options.label: It counts the petals to judge the centre
options.feedback: A bee has no way to count petals, and flowers vary too much in petal number for that to give a reliable answer.

options.label: It always lands on the same spot from memory alone
options.feedback: This works even on a flower a bee has never visited before, so memory of one particular flower cannot be the explanation.

items.ok_line: A path drawn in light a bee can see and we cannot.
items.ko_line: Think about a part of the light spectrum a bee's eyes can pick up that ours cannot.
items.exp_title: A pattern only a bee can see
items.exp_text: Many flowers carry markings on their petals made from pigments that reflect ultraviolet light, a part of the light spectrum a bee's eyes can detect but ours cannot. Those markings often form lines or a bullseye shape that stands out sharply against the rest of the petal and points inward toward the nectar, unlike the more uniform colour the same flower shows to us. Following that unmistakable path lets a bee reach the nectar directly instead of wandering randomly across the whole flower.

items.prompt: How can elephants far apart, out of sight and out of normal earshot of each other, still coordinate their movements?

options.label: They send scent signals carried on the wind
options.feedback: Scent fades and scatters over long distances and cannot carry a directional signal reliably across the distances involved here.

options.label: They rely on messages passed along by other animals
options.feedback: No other species carries information between elephants in this way; the communication is direct, from one elephant to another.

options.label: They stamp patterns on the ground that are read later
options.feedback: While elephants can sense certain ground vibrations, the coordination described here happens in real time over distance, not through a message left behind to be read afterward.

options.label: They produce and sense very low sounds beyond our hearing
options.feedback: Elephants can make deep rumbling calls pitched below the range of human hearing, and such low-frequency sound travels much farther through open ground and air than higher-pitched sound would, reaching other elephants far beyond normal earshot.

items.ok_line: A call pitched too low for us to hear, but not too low to carry.
items.ko_line: Think about a kind of sound that can travel much farther than an ordinary call.
items.exp_title: A call pitched too low to hear
items.exp_text: Elephants can produce deep, rumbling calls pitched below the range of ordinary human hearing, sounds so low that a person standing nearby might feel them as a faint vibration rather than hear them at all. Because low-pitched sound loses far less energy as it spreads than higher-pitched sound does, these calls can carry across open ground well beyond the distance any ordinary call could reach. Other elephants sense the calls partly through their ears and partly through vibrations felt in their feet and trunk, letting a herd stay coordinated across a landscape too vast for sight or normal hearing to cover.
